transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-03-12
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Alex Rivera (Redwood SE), Priya Patel (Redwood Solutions Eng), Tom Reynolds (CTO, Nimbus), Sara Kim (ML Infra Lead), Javier Ortega (SRE), Priya Singh (Head of Data)
Shared artifacts: autoscaling-deck.pdf (Redwood), sample-benchmark-config.yml (Redwood), Nimbus 7-day-telemetry.csv (to be shared)

[00:00] Maya (AE): ok hey everyone thanks for carving out the time today, we want to make this a pragmatic session — dig into autoscaling and capacity planning for the workload you described in the form. quick intros?
[00:10] Tom (CTO): yeah hi Tom here, we run Nimbus's realtime analytics pipelines, biggest pain is unpredictable surges during market open and certain enterprise customers. want to understand reserved vs burst pool tradeoffs.
[00:22] Sara (ML Infra): Sara — we manage the infra and the cost center, so curious about unit economics and also about cold-start behavior in a VPC setup.
[00:30] Javier (SRE): Javier — SRE, mostly about queueing/backpressure and SLOs.
[00:35] Maya (AE): awesome. alex from our SE team will lead through the runtime implications. alex?
[00:40] Alex (SE): thanks. quick agenda: 1) autoscaling primitives and policies, 2) queueing models and burst capacity, 3) caching/kv warmup and batching interactions, 4) quantization and perf tradeoffs, 5) VPC/on-prem implications and recommendations. we'll leave time for Q&A.

[01:05] Alex (SE): so at a high level Redwood supports two main capacity constructs: reserved GPU pools (dedicated capacity you commit to) and burst pools (shared or on-demand capacity that can be used when reserved is saturated). the autoscaler is policy driven — you can tune thresholds on effective queue length, p95/p99 latency, and token/sec consumption.
[01:25] Sara (ML Infra): can you define "queue length" as you use it — is it number of requests, or estimated token backlog?
[01:30] Alex (SE): good question — we expose both. default is request-count queue, but for mixed sequence-length workloads we provide tokenized backlog estimate (i.e., outstanding tokens to be served). that helps avoid overscaling for many short requests vs few very long ones.

[02:05] Alex (SE): we also support weighted priority queues — so enterprise customers can mark routes as high-priority which get preemptive slots in the runtime when bursting. this interacts with SLA-driven autoscaling so the controller will bias scale-up to ensure high-priority SLOs.

[02:38] Tom (CTO): how do burst policies affect cost? if we rely on burst pool for 10% of traffic, is that materially more expensive?
[02:45] Maya (AE): short answer: burst is typically priced higher per-token than reserved, but you only pay for it when used. for Nimbus's pattern we can model cost — send us the qps traces and seq len distribution and we’ll show a cost tradeoff.

[03:15] Alex (SE): important: burst capacity provisioning — we have two flavors: fast warm (warm VM with loading + KV cache cold) and cold cold (cold starts where model weights need to load). fast-warm usually adds ~500ms-3s depending on model and quantization; cold cold can be multiple seconds. so if you need strict sub-200ms p95 you need to provision more reserved GPUs or pre-warm.

[04:02] Sara (ML Infra): is that warm time improved by quantization or faster NVMe?
[04:06] Alex (SE): quantized models have smaller weights so they reduce load time; kernel selection impacts it too. NVMe vs networked storage helps—if models are on local NVMe the load is faster. for VPC customers we recommend pre-loading hot models into a warm pool if sub-second tail latency is required.

[04:40] Javier (SRE): let's talk about KV cache — our main use is chat-style apps with long context. warm KV cache seems critical. how do you handle cache warmup and how long does it persist after inactivity?
[04:52] Alex (SE): KV cache lifetime is policy-controlled. default TTL is 30 minutes but you can pin caches to a tenant or route; pinned caches survive scale-in events by keeping a small warm-shard. also we persist KV shards to a fast per-node cache so when a new pod spins up for burst it can fetch the relevant KV snapshot — fetch is typically 50-200ms depending on size and network.

[05:28] Sara (ML Infra): hmm 50-200ms extra on top of model load — that adds up. is it possible to pre-warm KV cache for known hot prefixes?
[05:34] Alex (SE): absolutely — we expose an API to pre-populate KV cache for a set of user prefixes. customers use it for prioritized accounts. we can also do lazy prefetch: when a request hits a cold pod it can asynchronously pull KV and serve a degraded faster path in parallel (e.g., approximate decoding).

[06:05] Tom (CTO): can we set autoscaler to scale on p99 latency rather than avg?
[06:09] Alex (SE): yes you can target p95 or p99. note p99-driven scaling is conservative and may increase reserved commit. often we do a hybrid: scale on p95 but keep a small buffer of reserved GPUs sized to handle historical p99 bursts or use priority queues for critical routes.

[06:35] Priya Singh (Head of Data): what about batching — we thought batching always increases throughput but hurts latency. how do you balance?
[06:42] Alex (SE): continuous batching is one of our runtime features: it batches across requests with a max batch size and max batching delay. you can set target latency SLO and the runtime will adapt the batching delay to hit it. For example, if target p95 is 300ms, the system will cap the batch delay to stay under that. for throughput-optimized routes you can increase max delay to get better GPU utilization.

[07:20] Javier (SRE): how do you handle backpressure? e.g., when queue grows beyond threshold, do you shed, queue, or route to fallback models?
[07:27] Alex (SE): we support several policies: 1) rate-limit + shed (reject), 2) graceful degrade (route to smaller/quantized model), 3) queue with SLA-based priority. routing to fallback models is a common pattern — you can define a chain: primary -> quantized -> cached summary response. Redwood's routing can do automatic fallback with user-defined thresholds.

[08:05] Tom (CTO): fallback to quantized models — what's typical quality delta?
[08:09] Alex (SE): depends on model and task; for completion tasks we see small degradation for 4-bit quantization on many open models, but for sensitive tasks you may not accept that. we provide a canary rollout and eval hooks so you can test quality on a held-out prompt set before automating fallback.

[08:40] Sara (ML Infra): From the infra perspective, what do the autoscaler metrics look like? we want to integrate into our alerting.

[08:47] Alex (SE): we emit metrics: current_replicas, pending_requests, token_backlog, avg_batch_size, p50/95/99 latency, kv_cache_hit_rate, model_load_time, and cost_estimate. you can forward to your Prometheus/Datadog; we supply Grafana/dashboards.

[09:20] Priya Patel (Redwood Solutions Eng): example pattern we've seen: reserve enough GPUs to handle baseline 80-90% traffic, configure burst pool for the remaining 10-20% with a fast-warm pre-warmed set sized for worst-case 5 min spike. that plus priority queues for enterprise routes keeps cost predictable while protecting SLOs.

[09:50] Tom (CTO): can you quantify "fast-warm pre-warmed set" — how many GPUs for long-tail spikes?

[09:55] Alex (SE): depends on model and request distribution. conservative rule: size warm-shard to handle your 95th percentile spike in QPS after batching. e.g., if after batching you need 1000 tokens/sec and your model does 200 tokens/sec per GPU, you'd need ceil(1000/200)=5 GPUs. we can run a profiler with your telemetry and give exact numbers.

[10:30] Sara (ML Infra): what about node packing and multi-tenant noisy neighbors? we run in a VPC and want isolation.

[10:37] Alex (SE): Dedicated pools give tenant isolation — you get dedicated instances and we don't pack other tenants on them. For shared burst pools we use soft isolation and cgroups; we also support burst-only dedicated slices if you want both isolation and burst elasticity.

[11:00] Javier (SRE): network egress and model artifact pulls — for on-prem or VPC we want to pre-load and avoid external pulls. what's the recommended pattern?

[11:08] Alex (SE): for VPC/private deployments we recommend using our artifact bucket mirror inside your network or an on-prem model store. preload hot models on nodes and use the warm pool to keep weights in memory. we also support an init container pattern for on-prem to fetch weights at startup from your internal registry.

[11:40] Tom (CTO): any gotchas with KMS or encryption overhead in VPC?

[11:45] Maya (AE): KMS operations are minimal and mostly at key fetch time; we recommend caching decrypted model keys in an HSM-backed process to avoid per-request decryption. we'll share our security integration docs.

[12:05] Alex (SE): another important detail: autoscaler cooldowns. scale-up is fast (seconds to minutes) but scale-down needs a conservative cooldown to avoid thrash. we recommend 5-10 minute min-retention for scaled replicas in most bursty markets; shorter for stable workloads.

[12:42] Sara (ML Infra): ok explain a sample controller config we might use.

[12:46] Alex (SE): sample: 1) target metric: token_backlog < 500 tokens; 2) scale-up policy: add 1 replica when p95>300ms for 30s or token_backlog>1000; 3) scale-down: remove replica if avg_utilization<40% for 10min; 4) reserve: commit 4 GPUs baseline; 5) burst: allow up to 8 on-demand with fast-warm pool of 2 pre-warmed. we'll send the JSON.

[13:30] Tom (CTO): can we do predictive scaling for scheduled spikes? we have predictable daily peaks.

[13:35] Alex (SE): yes we have scheduled/predictive scaling where you can upload expected t+window profiles and the controller pre-scales. combine that with pre-warming KV caches for accounts you know will spike.

[14:05] Priya Singh (Head of Data): curious about the queueing math — do you model as an M/M/c queue or more complex?

[14:12] Alex (SE): the runtime uses an approximate queuing model combining M/G/c characteristics with empirical service time distributions. we simulate expected tail latencies and can run Monte Carlo given your trace to estimate p95/p99 under different configs. it's not theoretical-only; we calibrate off live telemetry.

[14:50] Javier (SRE): ok let's talk SLA violations and mitigations — if a GPU node fails during a spike what happens to requests in flight?

[14:58] Alex (SE): runtime has request-level retries and a transparent fallback path. requests routed to the failed node are requeued (if within timeout) and can be routed to fallback quantized model if timeouts approach. we also support sticky routing for KV-affine sessions; in that case we may prioritize sticky sessions to warm nodes.

[15:35] Maya (AE): quick note — we often recommend customers carve out a small always-on pool for KV-affine sessions to avoid frequent rehydration.

[15:45] Tom (CTO): what's the billing implication of keeping an always-on pool?

[15:49] Maya (AE): always-on pool is charged as reserved capacity; but it can dramatically reduce operational E2E latency and hidden cost of retries/fallbacks. depending on utilization it may actually reduce total cost versus overuse of burst.

[16:10] Alex (SE): on quantization impacts: 8-bit and 4-bit quant reduce memory and inference time; 4-bit can reduce latency and memory footprint substantially but sometimes needs specialized kernels and may change per-token latency. also beam/ sampling strategies affect throughput. we provide per-model quant profiles.

[16:45] Sara (ML Infra): do you do mixed precision runtime? like run attention in fp16 and matmuls in int8?

[16:50] Alex (SE): yes kernels can be mixed -- we auto-select best kernel given the quantization and hardware; some performance gains come from fused attention kernels and optimized CUDA paths.

[17:15] Priya Patel (Redwood Solutions Eng): small real example — customer A shifted from reserved-only to 70/30 reserved/burst and saw 18% cost drop while keeping p95 under SLA by pre-warming two GPUs and pinning KV for top 20 accounts.

[17:45] Tom (CTO): good. let's dig into the benchmark you mentioned. what should we send?

[17:50] Alex (SE): ideally: 7-day qps trace (timestamp, seq_len, route), a representative prompt set for eval, and a sample of KV sizes. we'll run a replay on a staging cluster and produce profiles: model_load, kv_fetch, per-token latency, realized batch sizes.

[18:20] Javier (SRE): can the replay simulate warm and cold paths? we need to see worst-case cold-start latencies on burst.

[18:25] Alex (SE): yes we simulate both: cold start (model unloaded), fast-warm (weights loaded but kv cold), and warm (kv and weights ready). we'll include hit/miss mixes to show end-to-end p99.

[19:00] Sara (ML Infra): any recommended tooling to transform our traces into your replay format?

[19:05] Alex (SE): we have a small script in the sample-benchmark-config.yml that maps your logs to the replay format; we'll include it in the follow-up email.

[19:30] Priya Singh (Head of Data): couple of policy questions: 1) can we set different cooldowns per route? 2) can we have per-tenant cost caps?

[19:36] Alex (SE): yes to both. you can set per-route scale policies and per-tenant spend caps with automated throttles. spend cap triggers are configurable and can route traffic to cheaper fallbacks when exceeded.

[20:00] Tom (CTO): about the scenario where we have high variance — what's your recommended reserve % for finance-like spikes?

[20:06] Alex (SE): finance spikes tend to be short and sharp — we recommend 60-80% reserved for safety and a well-sized fast-warm burst to cover the rest. alternatively, predictive scaling for market-open windows can reduce the reserved footprint. we'll model both.

[20:30] Maya (AE): a couple of compliance notes: for on-prem/VPC deployments we support SAML SSO, SOC2 reports, and KMS integrations; we'll attach our security packet.

[20:45] Sara (ML Infra): about logging — retention and cost? we need audit logs and token-level billing but don't want to store heavy payloads.

[20:55] Maya (AE): you can configure log sampling and retention per-route; we also stream structured summaries instead of full payloads for billing and monitoring. we'll share config samples.

[21:20] Alex (SE): ok back to queueing — a visual I like is to think of two dimensions: time-to-serve (service time distribution) and backlog size. autoscaler uses those to compute risk of SLO miss and decides scale actions. we can send a Monte Carlo report for your trace.

[21:48] Javier (SRE): what about multi-region routing? if one region saturated you route to another — how do you handle latency and data residency?

[21:55] Alex (SE): smart routing can prefer same-region for latency and fall back to other regions when capacity constrained but only if policies allow cross-region processing; for data residency you can create routing policies that forbid cross-region routing for certain tenants.

[22:20] Tom (CTO): excellent. any last blockers you see for us to run a pilot?

[22:25] Maya (AE): none we can't manage — main blockers are: telemetry export, access to a representative prompt set, and decision on an initial reserved commit. once we have those we run the benchmark and propose a pilot config.

[22:45] Tom (CTO): sounds good. let's discuss the pilot sizing — we are leaning toward 4 reserved GPUs with 4 on-demand burst, but want your benchmark to validate.

[23:00] Alex (SE): we'll run simulation and a 24h bump test to validate the 4+4 config against your traces. we'll include KV warmup tests.

[23:20] Priya Patel (Redwood Solutions Eng): operationally, for the bump test we recommend doing it on a mirrored staging cluster with identical networking to emulate VPC egress and model fetch times.

[23:40] Sara (ML Infra): ok scheduling — let's do the follow-up scoping on 2025-03-20 and get the telemetry to you by 03-14.

[24:00] Maya (AE): great, last quick Qs?

[24:05] Tom (CTO): one more — in the scenario of degraded network to artifact store, do you have fallback to a minimal model?

[24:12] Alex (SE): yes fallback chains can include a minimal local model that provides a short canned response or summary. it's configurable per-route.

[24:30] Priya Singh (Head of Data): thanks — helpful.

[24:34] Maya (AE): wrap up: we'll send autoscaling deck, sample config, replay script, and run the benchmark. action items noted. thanks everyone.

[24:45] (meeting end)
